questions.text: Why distinguish an additive unknown field from an unknown resultType in this lesson’s modern response validation?

options.A: Both must always be discarded before the client sees the response.
options.B: An unknown resultType can always be inferred as complete.
options.C: Additive fields may be preserved or ignored, but an unknown discriminator implies a lifecycle the client cannot safely interpret.
options.D: Additive fields authorize extensions without any capability declaration.

questions.explanation: Forward-compatible fields do not necessarily change lifecycle semantics. An unknown or unadvertised resultType does, so the validator rejects it.

questions.text: A header-mismatch test triggers the local validator, but the actual origin response is HTTP500 with no JSON-RPC body. Has it proved the required server behavior?

options.A: Yes, because any failure proves the mismatch was rejected correctly.
options.B: No; it must capture and validate HTTP400 with the matching ID and JSON-RPC -32020.
options.C: Yes, if the SDK turns the response into a generic exception.
options.D: No; the server should silently choose the header value and continue.

questions.explanation: A local rejection alone tests the harness. Conformance requires the actual server wire response, including the expected HTTP status and correlated protocol error.

questions.text: validate_result({"tools": []}, era) infers complete only in its legacy branch and raises when a modern result lacks resultType. What happens with era="modern"?

options.B: It inserts resultType="complete" into the supplied dictionary.
options.C: It switches to the legacy branch because tools is an array.
options.D: It raises ProtocolViolation for missing resultType.

questions.explanation: The modern branch explicitly rejects a missing discriminator. Only a previously selected legacy era permits inference.
